description.en: Memory plugins for DeepSeek Harness: one unified surface, eight tools, one short standing injection.
description.zh: DeepSeek Harness 的记忆插件索引：一套统一工具面、一段最短常驻注入。

description.en: One memory plugin instead of three: 8 unified memory_* tools and a single 1,266-character injection, with meow-memory's seven-layer SQLite as the main store and a rebuildable graph index. Tool schemas 56,759 B → 14,494 B (−74.5%), standing prompt 4,085 → 1,266 chars (−69.0%). Nothing was dropped: writes land in the main store first, graph links that cannot be written are queued instead of lost, and the setting page takes effect without a restart. 0.4.0 adds query decomposition, write-time consolidation, supersede + inflation checks, an entity layer on the graph, and co-occurrence query expansion learned from your own keywords — every one of them has an off switch and an on/off reading. 0.5.0 bridges CJK word forms so a paraphrase still lands. 0.6.0 makes scoring scale-adaptive: on a 660-entry snapshot, verbatim hit@1 0.895 → 0.921 and paraphrased 0.333 → 0.417 with zero wrong flips, and every hit now carries its `status`. 0.6.1 turns the three-trees-out-of-sync problem into one command (`tools/sync-trees.mjs`, dry-run by default, never deletes), pins the adaptive-idf wiring with two static regexes so a silent behaviour regression cannot pass green, and fixes a `%20` path bug in a maintenance script — engine bytes unchanged. 0.6.2 fixes a recall bug where the store said nothing when something was there: the noise floor dropped the only matchable word and left a word that does not exist in the store in its place (8 of 1,531 English questions came back empty). It now rescues only the words the noise floor dropped and never function words, so empty replies went 0.52% → 0 while hit@1/5/10/20, MRR and the 660-entry snapshot readings stayed bit-identical. 0.6.3 makes answers reproducible: a tie on score used to fall back to corpus order (V8's stable sort), so the same question could give two different top-tens depending on how the store happened to lay the rows out. The ladder now ends with updated-later-first and a natural id order, the adaptive-idf cluster pick no longer breaks ties by array index, and no ordering step uses localeCompare — and every reading stayed bit-identical. 0.6.4 fixes single-character queries: the tokenizer only emits CJK bigrams, so a one-hanzi question yields no tokens and the retrieval gate treated “cannot tokenize” as “not in memory” — the most direct questions (`读`, `钱`, `花`) always came back empty. It now falls back to a literal substring pass over title/content/keywords only when the query is a single CJK code point and tokenization produced nothing, still going through the same ordering ladder; English stopwords and punctuation stay closed. Every reading is bit-identical — this restores reachability, not ranking. 0.6.5 fixes punctuated single-character queries: the 0.6.4 gate demanded exactly one code point, yet a one-hanzi question almost always carries punctuation — `读？`, `钱。`, `花！`, `「读」` all came back empty. The gate now strips punctuation and whitespace first and requires exactly one remaining hanzi, allowing only punctuation/whitespace beside it; letters, digits and symbols stay closed, and a repeated character counts once. Every reading is bit-identical again — reachability, not ranking. 0.6.6 fixes dirty memories: `...d.keywords` in `docText` threw `TypeError: d.keywords is not iterable` for entries whose keywords were missing, null, or a comma-joined string (imported rows, rows written by other plugins, caller-built docs) — not one missing hit, but a whole failed search. Keywords now go through `kwList`: arrays, comma/ideographic-comma strings and JSON strings all count, and `docText`, the scoring fields `kwToks`/`kwSets`, `keywordHitScore` and the index signature all use it (comma-joined keywords finally reach tf-idf). Every reading is bit-identical — reachability again, not ranking. 0.6.7 fixes broken rows: a single null / undefined / scalar entry in `docs` (half-written rows, truncated imports, a caller passing ids instead of objects) made `docText` throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'title')`, and a non-array `docs` died on `docs.length`. Both entry points now pass a gate `liveDocs(docs)`: non-arrays return empty, entries are checked for object-ness, filtering happens only when something is broken, and a clean array is returned as the same reference (the index cache is keyed by a content signature, not identity, so nothing is invalidated); an all-broken array returns empty rather than scoring null as a memory. Every reading is bit-identical. 0.6.8 is about the lifetime of the checks themselves: versions, suite counts, assertion totals and time budgets all advance every release, so writing them as equality turns every bump into a false failure (`0.2.31→35` hit it four times; `0.6.2→0.6.7` hand-bumped `steps.length === 35 → 36` each time and edited two hand-copied doc numbers). Suite count is now a floor (`SUITE_FLOOR`: adding a suite needs no edit, losing one fails immediately), the current numbers in the docs are reconciled automatically against the baseline totals, historical milestones keep their own numbers, and the version ladder is compared by version, not layout. The engine is byte-identical; every reading is the same. 0.6.9 measures the ruler first: since 0.3.0 every published reading came from a single pass in a single order (corpus in storage order, questions in fixture order), and those single-pass numbers are exactly what rejected three candidates (English stemming, MMR, coverage re-rank). If the ruler is order-sensitive, those negatives carry the ruler own noise. `tools/probe-rigor.mjs` now pins seven properties: three consecutive passes give bit-identical readings (std = 0), reversed corpus order, three shuffles (seed 3/11/42), reversed question order, a second independent scorer, an injected same-score-corpus-order bias that must go red (A/B top-1 hits 23 to 15), and fixed tier sizes 45/14/10. On 69 real-corpus questions: hit@1 0.9565 / hit@3 0.9855 / MRR 0.9686, unchanged across passes and orders. The engine is byte-identical; LoCoMo and real-corpus readings are unchanged. 0.6.10 removes a fixed per-query cost: the search-index cache key is a content signature, and while the usual answer is that the store did not change, the price was paid in full every time. On four isomorphic corpora (660 / 2,000 / 5,000 / 10,000) the signature consumed 28.8%-30.6% of a warm search (0.96 / 2.84 / 7.04 / 14.16 ms). It is now accounted per document: a WeakMap keyed by the doc holds a 32-bit per-doc hash plus a snapshot of the fields that feed it, compared by value (not object identity) before reuse; the per-doc hash had to be lifted out of the rolling value to be cacheable at all; shapes whose values cannot be compared fall back to direct computation. Signatures now cost 0.062 / 0.189 / 0.528 / 1.198 ms (15x, share down to 2.8%-3.5%) and a warm search 3.24 to 2.18, 9.67 to 6.80, 23.0 to 15.3, 49.2 to 37.6 ms. Ranking is byte-identical; LoCoMo and real-corpus readings are unchanged. 0.6.11 keeps paying down fixed cost: the remaining warm-search time is now accounted per channel, and the most expensive one is verbatim matching, which used to rebuild one lowercased string of the whole store on every query (id + project + title + content + keywords) just to answer whether an identifier appears verbatim, 2.03 MB at 10,000 docs and 35.7%-50.6% of a warm search; splitting that further showed 5.78 ms spent building strings against 0.51 ms of actual scanning. The haystack now lives in the index next to the token table, is built per document on demand and accounted (built / reused), and nothing is built when the query carries no identifier. The same change closed a 0.6.10 hole: the haystack contains project, project was never part of the signature, and once the string is cached a changed project would have been served from a stale index. Warm search: 2.04 to 1.62, 5.04 to 4.20, 11.88 to 9.12, 24.45 to 18.82 ms (-20.6% / -16.7% / -23.2% / -23.0%), verbatim share down to 18.6%-34.9%. Ranking is byte-identical; LoCoMo and real-corpus readings are unchanged. 0.6.12 keeps paying down fixed cost and targets the final ordering step. After the signature accounting of 0.6.10 and the verbatim accounting of 0.6.11, --cpu-prof attributed the largest remaining block to bandize (10,000 docs, 300 queries): to hand back the top ten it sorted the full hit list twice, once by _raw to assign bands and once by band, score, update time and id for the final order, while all three call sites only take the first k afterwards. Ordering was 40.3% of a warm search, about 11 ms per query, more than scanning documents. Band numbers are now written on the hit itself instead of a per-query Map, the comparator is factored into one orderOf ladder (band, then score, then more recently updated first, then natural id order) shared by both the full sort and the heap, and bandize takes a limit and selects the top k with a bounded max heap whose root is the worst selected hit; when the wanted count is not smaller than the total, the original full sort runs unchanged, so small stores and large k behave bit for bit as before. Bands and explain.band are only written on the surviving hits, and the temporary field is deleted. Search 27.377 to 19.985 ms (-27.0%), the production searchAdaptive path 31.086 to 23.097 ms (-25.7%), ordering share 40.3% to 21.5% (orderOf itself 0.9%), index reuse still 0.751 ms per query and cold index build unchanged at 270.7 ms. Ranking is bit-identical: the top k matches full-sort-then-slice across 500 random corpora and six k values, the total returned count stays 1,500, and LoCoMo plus the 52-question real-corpus readings are unchanged. 0.6.13 keeps paying down fixed cost and targets band assignment. After 0.6.12 capped ordering at the top k, a fresh --cpu-prof run (10,000 docs, 300 queries, 19.99 ms per search) showed the largest remaining block was still the full sort that exists only to assign bands: hits.slice().sort((a, b) => b[rawKey] - a[rawKey]) inside bandize, 21.5% of a warm search (bandize 10.9% plus the internal raw comparator 10.6%), paying comparator calls and object field reads for entries that can never reach the top k. Bands depend only on the distinct raw values after sorting, so the fix is three steps with identical semantics: copy raw values into a Float64Array and sort it with the native numeric sort (no comparator), walk it downward once to build a threshold chain (a0 is the maximum, a(i+1) is the largest value below 0.85 times a(i)), then binary-search each hit own value against the chain, where its band equals m minus 1 minus lo. Fallback: when any raw value is not a finite non-negative number (NaN, undefined, null, negative), the strictly decreasing anchor premise fails (0.85 times a negative value is larger, not smaller), so the whole pass falls back to the 0.6.13-era full sort setBandsBySort, and identified hits keep band minus one and stay out of the chain. Search 19.985 to 16.329 ms (-18.3%), the production searchAdaptive path 23.097 to 18.812 ms (-18.6%), band assignment share 21.5% to 7.8% (threshold chain 7.0% plus bandize 0.8%), index reuse still 0.703 ms per query, cold build 259 ms. Ranking is bit-identical: LoCoMo hit@1 0.3932, hit@5 0.6192, hit@10 0.6924, hit@20 0.7511, MRR 0.4958, recall@20 0.6322, zero empty answers, and the 52-question real-corpus readings match 0.6.12 exactly. 0.6.14 removes the leftovers from the hot path. After 0.6.13 cut band assignment from 21.5% to 7.8%, the function view only showed work being done (search self 45.8%, scanDoc 17.8%); a line-level attribution over cpuprofile positionTicks exposed the real cost: delete h._lv alone accounted for 791.5 ms, with delete h._vb and delete h._sr adding another 353 ms, so 1.14 s of a 5,671.8 ms sample went into removing values that had just been attached. The cause is four use-then-unset temporaries on each hit object (verbatim hit, pattern ratio, level intent, assertion density) that were cleaned up with delete, and delete pushes an object into dictionary mode, so every later property access, including the h._raw read inside the freshly optimized bandize, goes through a hash table; four saved assignments bought a slower whole path. Two changes keep semantics identical: the four temporaries move into parallel arrays indexed like hits (pushed right next to hits.push, read back by index), leaving the returned field set exactly as before; and idf is memoized per pass (within one pass idf is constant per term, so a per-query cache with idfAt yields bit-identical values without recomputing Math.log), with the cache reset when adaptive idf swaps its ruler. Two per-query allocations also disappear: raw.slice is only kept when explain is on, and the Math.max spread becomes a loop that preserves NaN propagation. Search 16.329 to 11.567 ms (-29.2%), or -57.7% against 27.377 ms in 0.6.12; the production searchAdaptive path 18.812 to 13.520 ms (-28.1%); zero delete calls left on the hot path, index reuse 0.679 ms per query, cold build 275 ms. Ranking is bit-identical: LoCoMo hit@1 0.3932, hit@5 0.6192, hit@10 0.6924, hit@20 0.7511, MRR 0.4958, recall@20 0.6322, zero empty answers, and the 52-question real-corpus readings match 0.6.13 exactly. 0.6.15 stops recomputing coverage per candidate. After 0.6.14 removed the 1.14 s of delete work, the function view again only showed work being done (search self 40.6%, scanDoc 18.8%); the line view named the cost: inside scanDoc the most expensive line was coverage, the loop that walks the query terms for every candidate and adds the idf of each term the document contains, at 573.9 ms over 300 queries, or 1.9 ms per query. The quantity itself is simple, the share of the query covered by a document, weighted by idf, but the algorithm was two-dimensional: for each candidate (up to 10,000) the full query vocabulary (dozens of terms) was asked again through a Map, hundreds of thousands of hash lookups per query just to produce 10,000 numbers, while the inverted index already records which documents each term appears in. Four changes keep semantics identical: per-query term idf is computed once into two Float64Arrays and read directly by the scoring loop; coverage is accumulated along the inverted index (a zero table sized by the document count, filled in the original query-term order, leaving one clamped division inside scanDoc), and because the addition order is unchanged every candidate keeps a bit-identical floating-point sum; when the inverted index is absent (explicitly disabled, or the query carries identifiers) the old per-candidate lookup path returns unchanged; and the candidate loop takes one record reference up front instead of re-resolving the same fields. The adaptive-idf ruler swap now re-accumulates both accounts in a fixed order: clear the idf cache, refresh term weights, rebuild the coverage table, then rescan. Search 11.567 to 10.673 ms (-7.8%), or -61.0% against 27.377 ms in 0.6.12; the production searchAdaptive path 13.520 to 12.522 ms (-7.4%); the coverage line 573.9 to 14.9 ms and scanDoc self time 23.8% to 18.8%; index reuse 0.698 ms per query and cold build 271 ms are flat within noise. Ranking is bit-identical: LoCoMo hit@1 0.3932, hit@5 0.6192, hit@10 0.6924, hit@20 0.7511, MRR 0.4958, recall@20 0.6322, zero empty answers, and all 52 real-corpus questions keep their scores and the two rank swaps. 0.6.16 stops looking up the term table for every candidate. After 0.6.15 removed the 573.9 ms of coverage work, the function view again only showed work being done (search self 48.0 percent, sigDocOf 9.5 percent, banding 7.5 percent); the line view named the next cost: the scoring loop that asks a Map for each query term of each candidate, 535.3 ms over 300 queries, about 1.8 ms per query. The quantity is term frequency times rarity times whether the hit was in the title or the keywords, and the first two inputs are fixed at index time; the inverted index already records which documents each term appears in. Three changes keep semantics identical: the inverted value grows from a list of document indexes to three parallel lists (index, term frequency, field-hit bits), with frequency and bits pushed in the same document-loop order so they stay index-aligned, and field weights are never multiplied into the index because they are per-query options that callers can override, so only the hit bits are stored and the weight is applied on the hot path; scoring runs the other way round, first preparing per-candidate constants (coverage, the length-normalisation denominator, the coordination term) and then, in the original query-term order, letting each term touch only the documents that contain it, adding its saturated term score to the raw score, so every candidate receives its addends in the same order and keeps a bit-identical floating-point sum; the finishing pass then applies synonyms, the coordination term and the entity layer per candidate with the same arithmetic as before; and the per-candidate path is untouched, still serving the case where the inverted index is disabled or the query carries identifiers. Search 10.67 to 8.35 ms (-21.8 percent, or -69.5 percent against 27.38 ms in 0.6.12), the production searchAdaptive path 12.52 to 10.16 ms (-18.9 percent), profiler samples 4,143.7 to 3,295.9 ms (-20.5 percent) with scanDoc gone from the top 25, index reuse still 0.69 ms per query. One cost, paid once: cold build 269 to about 300 ms, roughly 11 percent more, because each term stores two extra lists. One bug worth recording: the candidate list was not cleared at function entry, so the adaptive ruler swap pushed every candidate a second time and the finishing pass applied its factors twice, visible as an unchanged per-candidate path next to a shifted adaptive path. Ranking is bit-identical: LoCoMo hit@1 0.3932, hit@5 0.6192, hit@10 0.6924, hit@20 0.7511, MRR 0.4958, recall@20 0.6322, zero empty replies, and the 52-query real-store snapshot keeps all three tiers plus its two rank swaps. 0.6.17 trims the hit object before hydrating it. After 0.6.16 moved scoring onto the inverted index, search self time fell from 48 to 9 percent, and the most expensive remaining lines were no longer algorithm work but the receipt object literal itself: the scan loop built a fourteen-field hit for every candidate (level, title, content, importance plus five optional pass-through fields, with four conditional spreads), 134 to 176 ms per line and about 1.07 s over 300 queries, two thirds of the self time, while banding and trimming keep only the top k, so the plugin paid a full object for each of the thousands of entries destined to be dropped. Three changes keep semantics identical: the scan phase carries only what banding needs (subject, raw, cover, id, updated_at and score) plus an internal index, since band assignment and ordering read nothing else; after truncation the surviving k entries are hydrated back to the full object in the original key order, taking the score already on the lean object, because identifier bonus, level intent, assertion density and status digest have already been applied to it and recomputing would lose them, and replacing array elements in place rather than building a new array so the trimmed and rescueAdded properties survive; the explain and keepBand paths keep the full literal, since the former patches the object in place and the latter must keep the band for fusion. Search 8.35 to 3.5 ms (-58 percent, or -87 percent against 27.38 ms in 0.6.12), searchAdaptive 10.16 to 4.5 ms (-54 percent), profiler samples 3,295.9 to 1,808.2 ms, index reuse still 0.69 ms per query, cold build unchanged at 288 to 301 ms. Ranking is bit-identical: LoCoMo hit@1 0.3932, hit@5 0.6192, hit@10 0.6924, hit@20 0.7511, MRR 0.4958, recall@20 0.6322, zero empty replies, and the 52-query real-store snapshot keeps all three tiers plus its two rank swaps. A new probe covers six checks: the lean path and the full path are byte-identical after dropping explain, key order included, the keepBand path matches after peeling internal fields, no internal fields leak while the array properties remain, optional fields are still omitted or passed through, and both paths agree on a large corpus. 0.6.18 drops Set from the candidate set. After 0.6.17 trimmed and hydrated hit objects, a hot search costs 3.49 ms, and the top functions are all per-query fixed costs over ten thousand entries, while the candidate set was still paying an avoidable price: the inverted-index path merged the entries hit by query terms and their co-occurrence expansions into a Set with two add rounds and iterated it, 137.4 ms or 7.6 percent per line, followed by the scoring function at 112.2 ms, all spent on hashing and iterator allocation, when the semantics need only two things: an index-to-seen lookup and first-seen ordering. Two changes, identical semantics: deduplication becomes a Uint8Array bitmap, with the two dedup sites reading if (candAt[di] === 0) { candAt[di] = 1; candList.push(di); }, one for query terms and one for expansions; the candidate table keeps first-seen order, and the scoring function loops by index, with length normalization, the coverage table, the candidate array and both null checks, first pass and rescaled pass, now testing the candidate table. The fallback is untouched: with the inverted index off or an identifier in the query the bitmap is null and the full scan runs. Bit-identical because first-seen order is exactly the insertion order of the set, the bitmap answers only seen-or-not, and push preserves order, so the candidate array layout, scan order, floating point addition order and receipt order are unchanged. Search 3.49 to 3.01 ms (-13.7 percent, or -89 percent against 27.377 ms in 0.6.12), searchAdaptive 4.568 to 4.54 ms, profiler samples 1,808.2 to 1,678.4 ms, and the candidate block left the top twenty. Ranking is bit-identical: LoCoMo hit@1 0.3932, hit@5 0.6192, hit@10 0.6924, hit@20 0.7511, MRR 0.4958, recall@20 0.6322, zero empty replies, and the 52-query real-store snapshot keeps all three tiers plus its two rank swaps. A new probe covers six checks: the seven source facts including that Set has left the candidate block, a 200-case comparison of bitmap union against set union, bit-identical results with the inverted index on and off, that the synonym expansion path is really exercised because the trimmed counter goes from undefined to one while order is unchanged and only scores differ, an empty query never yields NaN, and 300 entries times 30 queries stay bit-identical on both paths. 0.6.19 removes the sort from band assignment. After 0.6.18 switched the candidate set to a bitmap, a hot search costs 2.98 ms, and the runner-up function is still band assignment at 235.6 ms or 14.0 percent, where the single most expensive line is the bulk sort at 164.9 ms, seventy percent of that function: the work is to walk ten thousand raw scores from high to low and open a new band whenever a value falls below 0.85 times the previous anchor, yet the anchor chain only consumes the distinct sorted values and was paying a comparison sort for every entry first. The cause is that band assignment needs a descending walk, not a total order. Three changes, identical semantics: the bucket key is the high thirty-two bits of the IEEE bit pattern shifted right by sixteen, since for non-negative finite doubles the bit pattern orders like the value, a sixteen-bit bucket is 6.25 percent wide, two values in one bucket differ by at least a factor of 0.941, far above one minus 0.85, so a bucket holds at most one anchor and its maximum suffices without sorting; counting sort gathers runs and then one walk over bucket numbers from high to low picks, per bucket segment, the largest value still below the threshold as the next anchor and skips a bucket whose whole segment is above it; bucket zero is special-cased because zero and all subnormals share it with no bound on relative spread, so that segment is copied out, sorted, and walked with the same chain, which is what makes corpora spanning ten to the plus or minus three hundred line up. One fallback: on a big-endian host the bit pattern no longer orders like the value, so the old sorted chain runs, sorting only the first n entries because the buffer is reused and its tail holds the previous round. Bit-identical because the chain definition is unchanged, buckets only change the order in which values are read, a bucket cannot hold a second anchor, the maximum is taken instead of a sorted value, bucket zero is really sorted, and the binary search in band assignment is untouched. Search 2.982 to 2.52 ms (-15.4 percent, or -90.8 percent against 27.377 ms in 0.6.12), searchAdaptive 4.105 to 3.51 ms, band assignment 235.6 to 74.0 ms (14.0 to 4.9 percent), the new helper itself only 28.5 ms or 1.9 percent, profiler samples 1,678.4 to 1,520.9 ms, and cold index builds stay at 292 to 299 ms. Ranking is bit-identical: LoCoMo hit@1 0.3932, hit@5 0.6192, hit@10 0.6924, hit@20 0.7511, MRR 0.4958, recall@20 0.6322, zero empty replies, and the 52-query real-store snapshot keeps all three tiers plus its two rank swaps. A new probe covers seven checks: source shape including that the bulk sort has left the threshold path, bit-identical anchors against the sorted chain on five hundred random corpora with zeros, duplicates, subnormals and values spanning ten to the plus or minus three hundred, a same-bucket ratio floor of 0.85 with a measured worst case of 0.943627, degenerate corpora, band-by-band comparison with identified rows excluded from the chain, a reused buffer that never bleeds, and bucket-number facts where zero and the smallest subnormal land in bucket zero and 1.0 lands in 16368. 0.6.20 removes the weak-map lookup from signature checking. After 0.6.19 dropped the sort from band assignment, a hot search costs 2.52 ms and the top function became the per-document signature reader at 265.5 ms or 16.4 percent: all it answers is whether this corpus is still the corpus from a moment ago, so it walks the document array once, compares eight fields per entry, folds them into one total signature, and uses that signature as the key of the search-index cache. The per-entry record it folds comes from a weak map keyed by the document object; the field comparison is cheap, the read is not. A ten-thousand-entry corpus pays ten thousand hash lookups per question, while a second visit to the same array finds every entry at the same index: what is needed is the previous verdict by index, what was paid is a hash lookup by object, and the same question even computed the signature twice. Two changes plus three things not to touch: first, an aligned row cache whose weak-map key is the document array itself, holding an array of rows aligned one-to-one with indices, each row holding the very same per-entry record object rather than a copy, so the read becomes an indexed element access; second, rows are only allocated on the second visit, because callers in the real store often hand in a freshly built array, where allocating ten thousand empty slots would be a regression. Untouched: the folding order, so the XOR and multiply still run in document order and the signature stays bit-identical, otherwise the cache key and the signature probes fail together; the counting contract, so a row hit still records a hit and a reuse and entries that are not objects, or whose fields are not scalars, or whose keywords hold non-scalars, keep an empty row and are computed fresh, otherwise two differently shaped dirty entries would collapse into one; and the path for non-array iterables, since anything other than an array has no index alignment to speak of. The question now computes the signature once and shares it between the cache key and the self-check. Readings on ten thousand same-shape entries over three hundred questions, median of three: search 2.522 to 2.042 ms, down 19.0 percent and 92.5 percent below 0.6.12 at 27.377 ms; searchAdaptive, which is what the product calls, 3.51 to 2.59 ms, down 26.1 percent; total profile samples 1,624.0 to 1,433.5 ms; the per-entry function left the leaderboard; the fresh-array path moved from 2.579 to 2.604 ms inside noise, so it does not regress; cold build stays at 291 to 297 ms. Not one answer moved: on LoCoMo, ten samples, five thousand eight hundred eighty-two turns, one thousand nine hundred eighty-six questions, the old and new engines agree on zero mismatches across the top twenty per question, and the real store keeps its three tiers at 0.921, 0.417 and 0.500 with both rank shifts intact. A new probe adds six checks: the shape, four thousand and eighteen bit-identical comparisons between the row-cached pass and the fresh-array pass, an identical counting contract on both paths, eight kinds of edits all visible, three consecutive calls agreeing and a copy agreeing, and dirty entries staying distinct. Its second check first failed for a measurement reason rather than a semantic one: two paths sharing one batch of document objects let the first fill the per-entry cache, so each path now gets its own same-shape corpus. 0.6.21 removes the per-character Unicode regex from lexical classification. After 0.6.20 moved signature checking to an aligned row cache, a hot search costs 2.04 ms, and unfolding the function view by line shows the costliest single line is not in search but in the small function that only answers whether a code point is Han, alphanumeric, or punctuation: 71.4 ms plus 16.2 ms, 88.7 ms or 6.2 percent for the function. The cause is plain: the verdict depends only on the code point, so it is a table lookup, yet the hot path runs two Unicode property regexes per code point, once per code point while tokenizing and again at every segment boundary, over the same corpus of ten thousand entries for every question. The fixes, plus three things not to touch: first, a code point table with three values for blank, Han, and alphanumeric, built by the same two regexes scanning their own contiguous runs, so equivalence is constructed rather than hand-transcribed; second, build it lazily, once, on the first classification, sixty-four kilobytes, then a single indexed read, while astral code points and lone surrogates still take the original regex path; tokenizing compares numbers instead of strings and the exported string classifier stays as a thin wrapper under the same name. Untouched: the table must be scanned out of the regexes, since the katakana prolonged sound mark and the ideographic iteration mark belong to common script and the alphanumeric class admits extra letters, so hand transcription always misses; the priority stays Han first then alphanumeric, with alphanumeric only filling still-blank cells; and astral code points stay out of the table, because it covers only the basic plane and anything outside must take the regex path or a surrogate pair would be split into two half code points. Readings, ten thousand entries and three hundred questions, median of three: search 2.042 to 2.000 ms, adaptive 2.593 to 2.528 ms, cold build 292 to 233.5 ms, total sampled time 1433.5 to 1337.0 ms, and the classifier drops off the profile. The real gain is in the cold build, not the hot question. Answers are unchanged: the real-store fifty-two question suite keeps 0.921, 0.417, and 0.500 with the same rank movements, and LoCoMo with ten samples, 5882 turns, and 1986 questions matches on the top twenty for every question across old and new engines. Not one answer byte changed: cold build four hundred sixty two items, tokenizer fifteen thousand eight hundred ten, search two thousand four hundred sixty two, plus a fast path ruler of three thousand eight hundred sixty eight, all with zero mismatches; in process the fast path and explain mode, which runs the old post processing, were compared band by band across eight distributions times six queries for forty eight identical pairs; a fixed corpus times eight queries produced the same receipt fingerprint as 0.6.29, 0.6.30, 0.6.31 and 0.6.32. New checks: three hot path probes for the logarithmic shape, band for band equality between fast and old routes, and monotone bands with equal scores sharing a band, plus forty eight in process pairs, monotonicity, the fingerprint and the docs. Assertion total went from 3,906 to 3,916. 0.6.34 attacks per query constants and the storage shape of the candidate table. After the previous release moved the position guess onto a bit level logarithmic ruler, the profile totalled four thousand seven hundred twenty two point nine milliseconds, and the top lines inside the search, whose own time was one thousand seven hundred seventy seven milliseconds, were all independent of what the query asked: candidate deduplication at one hundred thirty six point six milliseconds, the recency weight call at one hundred fourteen, and the decay guard at ninety six point eight. Two falsifications came first. Flattening those small functions into the hot loop was worth zero point six percent, because the engine already inlines unary helpers like these and the profile charges the call site, not the call; and turning the signature row from one record object per row into five string arrays plus two float arrays plus keyword arrays flattened more slowly, nine point nine eight against nine point zero seven nanoseconds per row over ten thousand uniform rows with three hundred passes and five rounds by median, since rows allocated in sequence are adjacent memory already and there is no cache miss to save, so the signature structure was left alone. The damage was in three places: the candidate set was an array with pushes plus a full copy handed downstream, which meant eight thousand seven hundred growth steps and one copy per query; the recency decay divided the millisecond delta by a day in milliseconds before comparing, a division that is pure overhead because the per day band edges converted to milliseconds are bit identical to the original test with a split window around one hundred millionth of a millisecond; and the decay guard read the document object for importance first, when candidates already above the current best score never needed the comparison at all. The fix is four per query constants plus two shapes: the candidate table becomes a fixed length integer array with a cursor, and the pure copy disappears with it; the recency ladder steps in milliseconds; importance and status weights are flattened into the loop; the complement of the coordination constant is hoisted; the guard compares the read only score array before touching the document; and token lengths are laid out as an integer array at index time so scoring no longer reads lengths back. Readings: fixed ten thousand rows, three thousand queries, top five, one process per engine alternating three rounds by median, the hot search went from one point one seven two five to one point zero eight five six milliseconds per query, down seven point four percent, with pairs at five point nine, seven point six and six point six; the first four items alone gave one point one seven four eight to one point one three seven six, or three point two, and the last two took another four point two. The new profile totals four thousand four hundred fifty seven point six milliseconds, search self one thousand six hundred fifty eight point one against one thousand seven hundred seventy seven, candidate deduplication one hundred twenty point three against one hundred forty six point two, the decay guard eighty three point five against one hundred eleven, the length penalty inside scoring two hundred eight point one against two hundred forty six, and buffer pickups per query went from six places to seven. Not a single answer moved: cold build four hundred sixty two items, tokenization fifteen thousand eight hundred ten, search two thousand four hundred sixty two, plus the fast path ruler at three thousand eight hundred sixty eight, all with zero mismatches; the fast path and the explain mode were compared band by band in process over eight distributions times six queries, forty eight pairs all identical; and the digest of eight queries over the fixed corpus is the same string as in 0.6.29 through 0.6.33. Three hot path checks were added: the candidate table shape, the millisecond ladder over ten bands with plus or minus one millisecond edges landing identically, and reuse without cross talk; plus the forty eight in process pairs, monotonicity, the digest and the documentation check. Assertion total went from 3,916 to 3,926. 0.6.35 attacks the document identity that the search entry rebuilt on every query. After the previous release the signature branch still took one thousand one hundred ninety nine point six milliseconds in the profile, but all three ways to change the signature itself were falsified: inlining the per row check was worth five percent, flattening the per row record object was slower at nine point nine eight against nine point zero seven nanoseconds per row, and skipping the check would bet correctness on an assumption nobody guards. Asking the question differently found the damage at the entry: the search handler mapped every database row into a fresh document object and packed them into a fresh array on each query, while both engine caches key on identity, one per document object and one per array that only fills rows on the second visit of the same array, so every query rehashed the whole library of content, title and keywords. Production measurement over ten thousand rows and six hundred queries: reusing the same batch costs one point one zero seven two milliseconds per query against twelve point five nine six five when rebuilding, a factor of eleven point four; no benchmark could see this layer because they all reuse one array, which is exactly the premise that never holds in production. The fix is three pieces: reuse document objects by identifier plus a ten field fingerprint with a cap of twenty thousand entries trimmed in insertion order, keep a single document array and patch it in place when cells change so its identity never changes, and expose two accounting columns for reuse versus fresh objects and returns versus patches. The first version only returned the old array when it matched and built a new one otherwise, and the per query hit count update killed it immediately: it raises the last access time of every hit, so the rows read back for the next query always differ in a few places, which made every query a fresh array and invalidated the whole row cache; the row cache freshness fields do not include the last access time, so as long as the array identity holds those touched rows never get rehashed. The historical boost pool path is deliberately left alone. Readout: production shape including the hit count update, two engine generations in alternating processes, three rounds by median, from eleven point four zero two eight down to two point zero six nine nine milliseconds per query, eighty one point nine percent or five point five one times, rounds at two point zero five six three, two point zero six nine nine and two point zero nine five three, with identical hit digest strings; cache ledger of twelve thousand nine hundred ninety five fresh objects against eight million nine hundred eighty seven thousand and five reuses, and arrays created once, returned three hundred times, patched five hundred ninety nine times over two thousand nine hundred ninety five cells. Engine level warm median went from one point one three eight to one point zero three three milliseconds and cold from one hundred thirty point five eight to one hundred twenty nine point five seven with no regression. Not one answer moved: cold build four hundred sixty two, tokenization fifteen thousand eight hundred ten, search two thousand four hundred sixty two and the fast path ruler three thousand eight hundred sixty eight all show zero mismatches; signatures are bit identical to the rebuild path including comma string, null and single element keyword shapes; reused document objects serialize unchanged after nine hundred searches; and the reply fingerprint matches 0.6.29 through 0.6.34. Eight new identity criteria were added: shape, reuse counts, any of ten fields changing must produce a new object, identical signatures, cap accounting, dirty rows surviving, constant array identity, and a production ratio of at least two with the hit count update in play. Assertion total went from 3,926 to 3,942. 0.6.36 and 0.6.37 ship as one batch on two lines: one removes the per query whole library signature check by construction, the other turns the synonyms already written inside the library into retrieval force. 0.6.36 fixes the signature check: after the previous release indexSignature still took three thousand and twenty milliseconds, one millisecond per query, while the stable document step already compared identifier, title, content, time and keywords field by field and then threw the conclusion away, so the signature branch rehashed the whole library on every query. The fix lets the conclusion travel with the object: docStepOf writes it into a module level slot, the stable document array seals itself with a version (length, version, signature version and the last signature string), and indexSignature returns the cached string whenever the signature version matches the current one, bumping the version only when a signature field really changed; last access time, importance, status and level never bump it. The contract is documented: do not mutate fields of documents produced by the stable array, which the engine never does and the probe rechecks every round. Production measurement over ten thousand rows and six hundred queries with hit count updates, alternating processes three rounds and taking the median, went from two point zero six five six to one point five zero four six milliseconds per query, twenty seven point two percent and a factor of one point three seven, or eight point two eight against 0.6.34; object and array accounting is identical, the hit string digest is byte identical, and all four rulers report zero mismatches at four hundred sixty two cold builds, fifteen thousand eight hundred ten tokenizations, two thousand four hundred sixty two searches and three thousand eight hundred sixty eight fast path checks. 0.6.37 fixes capability: paraphrase recall in a cold domain had zero first place hits, because every domain carries one colloquial mapping row that collects the whole spoken vocabulary on a single line, short and dense with the highest coverage by nature, pushing the real answer to second or third place. The fix gives such a row two identities: a self learned synonym source, mining A equals B pairs bidirectionally and splitting both sides into bigram keys because scoring works on bigrams and not whole words, and a demoted candidate that is multiplied by zero point two five when judged a mapping row by pair count and symbol density; terminology questions are exempt, and an explicit mapping outranks statistical co-occurrence, which steps aside when a declared pair exists. Paraphrase first place rose from zero to seventy percent, top three from eighty to ninety, MRR from zero point three four two to zero point eight; the five fixture domains yield eighteen pairs and five correctly demoted rows, the real library yields forty eight pairs and zero demotions, same word queries stay at one hundred percent, and ablations are now assertions: without the bridge recall collapses to zero, without any expansion it holds thirty percent. Assertion total went from 3,942 to 3,978. 0.6.38 gives the injection a budget: injectMaxChars (default 0 = unlimited, so the old byte-for-byte layout is untouched) caps standing and per-hit injection, keeps every entry header, drops an entry entirely rather than leaving a bare id, states how much it squeezed, and on a real corpus of seven entries (1,415 chars in total) cuts 69.1% at 600 chars and 80.2% at 400 while keeping 2/7 and 1/7 entries whole. The graph neighbourhood now filters weak links (neighborMinScore 0.35) and, when a neighbour is plainly irrelevant, the injection tail names the source id and tells the model to inspect the path and mute the wrong hop - a curated mute takes effect immediately and survives rebuilds. 0.6.39 fixes same-domain lexical interference: a question whose wording hits another entry in the same domain leaves the real answer without literal evidence, because that answer carries an internal term. Paraphrase recall on the cold-domain ruler went from 70 percent to 90 percent first place, 90 percent to 100 percent top three and MRR from 0.800 to 0.950. Two root causes: a synonym declared by a glossary row (A equals B) only earned the expansion weight 0.6 and no title or keyword field bonus, while a class name matching a title earned 1.95; and an out-of-vocabulary word had no entry at all, because the index stores bigrams. Four fixes, each with a switch: declared counterparts get full weight plus field bonuses (synWLookup, default 1); an ambiguous class name is discounted per query term (declDirectW, default 0.7, null when nothing is declared); a glossary row stops earning field bonuses, so a terminology table cannot outrank the answer it defines; and a head-morpheme bridge (charBridge, charBridgeW 0.3) indexes keywords by their final character, fills only entries whose direct score is zero, counts only when the bridge lands on a title or a keyword, requires a literal anchor in the question, and sums several hits with a cap of three times the best one. Setting all four back returns 70 / 90 / 0.800 bit for bit, and the no-answer ruler stays at 10 of 14, so the new power is switchable and the old behaviour is intact. 0.6.40 puts a floor under routine recall injection. Hit injection used to be bounded only by a count (hitTopK, default 2) with no score threshold at all, so a plain operational question could pull in a memory that merely shared one keyword token: on a real 824-entry library, 11 of 13 operational questions triggered injection, 9,049 characters in total, nearly all of it noise the model had to read and then discard. New switch injectFloor (default 0.45, 0 disables, old behaviour bit for bit): the gate reads the score keywordHitScore already produced instead of rescaling anything, blocked entries are not marked as seen and do not bump hit_count so a stronger hit can still arrive on a later turn, renderHitEntries, markInjected and bumpHit all act only on what survived the gate, and both the receipt (budget.floor, budget.gated) and the hit-chain log line (floor, gated) report what was cut. The 0.45 line comes from a self-hit experiment over the same 824 entries: every entry queried with its own top three keywords scores at the 1st percentile 2.046, so the line keeps 823 of 824, while twelve unrelated operational questions peak at 0.42 and none of them pass. Readings: the nine memory-related questions still inject on 9 of 9 turns while their text drops from 8,747 to 6,873 characters (21.4 percent saved, five weak tails gated); the thirteen operational questions drop from 11 of 13 turns and 9,049 characters to 2 of 13 turns and 1,668 characters (81.6 percent saved); setting injectFloor to 0 reproduces the old injection byte for byte. Bad values are handled in two documented ways: a non-number falls back to 0.45 rather than silently disabling the gate, and a negative number clamps to 0, which is an explicit opt-out. 0.6.41 caps the body of one injected memory. Hit injection was bounded in count, and since 0.6.40 in score, but a long entry was still pasted in whole on every turn it matched: on a real 824-entry library the body length is 248 characters at the median, 595 at p90 and 2,576 at the worst, and the longest entries are exactly the ones keywords match most often, so a typical turn carried a project topic of 596 characters plus a fact of 401 characters while only a sentence or two of it was relevant. New switch injectBodyMax (default 240, 0 disables, old behaviour bit for bit): an over-long entry is digested into its opening sentence, the sentences that overlap the question, and any hard-information sentence (numbers, versions, paths, backticked identifiers); the entry header is never dropped and a memory_read(id) pointer line follows the digest so the full text stays one call away. Chinese sentence scoring was silently broken before this release: the tokenizer treated a whole run of Han characters as a single term, so every sentence scored zero and compression always degenerated into "keep the first sentence only"; terms are 2-grams now, which lets a question such as "how many neighbours by default" pick the right sentence out of the middle of an entry. Readings: the sweep over the same 824 entries trims 25.2 percent of injected text on memory-related questions and 28.3 percent on operational ones at the default, while the 0.6.40 gate accounting is untouched (probe-floor 30/30, probe-budget 34/34). Setting injectBodyMax to 0 reproduces 0.6.40 byte for byte. Bad values: a non-number falls back to 240, a negative number clamps to 0, which is an explicit opt-out. 0.6.42 puts the injection knobs on the settings page. Six numbers decide how much long-term memory is pasted into every turn: injectFloor (the hit relevance gate, 0.45), injectBodyMax (the per-entry body limit, 240), and the graph-neighbourhood quartet neighbour injection on/off, neighbours per turn (4), neighbourhood block budget (420) and neighbour strength floor (0.35). All six existed in the config file and none of them was reachable from the settings UI: the inject group offered only hitTopK, titleMax and injectMaxChars, and the graph neighbourhood had no group at all, so a user who wanted to spend fewer tokens had to hand-edit config.json, which in practice means the switch did not exist. The cause was not one forgotten line: each knob arrived in its own release with engine defaults, config defaults, a zod schema, config resolution, live-update keys and a probe, and none of those releases looked back at the panel. The panel code is a vendored upstream artifact with a recorded hash and a silent overwrite on upgrade, so hand edits neither show up in this repo diff nor survive. This release ships a build-time patch instead: tools/patch-settings-fields.mjs is applied by build.mjs while assembling the client bundle, with counting guards that throw when an anchor no longer matches. It adds thirteen localized strings in English, Chinese and Portuguese (label and hint for each knob plus the new group title), the six factory defaults, two fields in the inject group, a new graph-neighbourhood group, and the matching UI keys; a probe asserts the panel defaults equal the engine and fusion-layer defaults one by one. The same work uncovered a real bug: config resolution wrote the legacy nested macro section after the top-level keys, so a leftover nested value silently overrode whatever the user picked in the panel, with no error and no log line; the order is now nested first, top-level keys last, which is what the function comment and the meow section already promised. Two probes back this up: probe-settings (27 checks over bundle output, field shape, grouping, factory defaults, all three languages, UI keys, fusion-layer wiring and the override order) and a real-render upgrade of probe-client-ui (19 checks) that actually executes the settings component instead of asserting on source text, which is what catches a bundle that parses as data but not as code. The panel writes top-level keys, the change is picked up by the live-update event and rebuilds the neighbourhood injector within a debounce window. Remaining unchanged: not writing these six keys resolves to the same defaults as 0.6.41, and the reset button writes the engine defaults rather than a second copy of the numbers. 0.6.43 puts three gates on the graph-neighbourhood injector, because neighbours were sometimes simply irrelevant. The injector had three holes. First, the record of "which neighbours were already pasted" lived in an in-memory map keyed by session, so a host restart — or resuming the same session later — wiped it and the same neighbours were pasted again. Second, it only tracked what it had pasted itself and never looked at what the keyword-hit injection had already pasted in the same turn, so a single memory could appear twice in one conversation. Third, the strength floor (0.35) was the only test: entries that scored high enough but shared no wording at all with the question were still carried, leaving the model unable to tell which one to mute and which one was merely pulled in by the graph. The three fixes: (1) the record is now persisted to $DSH_HOME/macro-memory/neighbor-seen/<session>.json, with characters that are illegal in Windows file names replaced and the name capped at 96 characters; an unreadable file is treated as an empty record and a failed write only logs one line and retries next turn, never blocking the turn. (2) Cross-layer deduplication: injectedIdsOf(messages) recognises memory-injection messages among the last 400 messages, extracts their ids, and matches them by 8-character prefix, since the graph reports short ids and hit injection reports full ones; it deliberately does not import the meow plugin private ledger, which would bind this plugin to another plugin internals and break on upgrade — the conversation history itself is the more direct fact, and it also covers the resume-after-restart case. (3) A wording gate: neighbourTokens takes Chinese character bigrams plus whole Latin words, and any neighbour that shares no token with the question is subject to a quota of one per turn; a neighbour scoring 0.5 or above is exempt entirely, because zero wording overlap does not mean irrelevant — paraphrasing, switching language or a truncated summary can remove every bigram while the neighbour is still the most useful one in the graph. Calibration on the real graph (3,561 nodes, 16 real questions) is reported honestly rather than favourably: the wording gate changes nothing there, 36 entries and 3,770 characters both before and after, because the four zero-overlap neighbours all scored at least 0.5 and took the exemption, so this gate is a guardrail and not a token saver. Same-turn overlap between the two injectors measured zero out of 18 hit entries and 36 neighbour entries, so the value of that fix is that it cannot happen rather than that it saves a lot. The strength curve (0.35 to 36 entries and 2,792 characters over 12 turns, 0.45 to 28, 0.50 to 23, 0.60 to 15) leaves the default untouched, since the entries cut at 0.40 included genuinely relevant ones; users who want to spend less can raise the neighbour strength floor from the settings page added in 0.6.42. Falling back is trivial: calling the renderer without a query behaves exactly as in 0.6.42, and deleting the neighbor-seen directory returns to the in-memory behaviour. Persisting the ledger also broke the test suite in two honest ways that are now fixed: probes reuse fixed session ids, so the second run of the same probe found its own earlier entries and asserted the wrong thing, and the probe was writing scratch files into the real home directory; every probe now points DSH_HOME at a temporary directory and cleans up after itself. Self-checked by 59 suites / 4,178 executable assertions in about 300 seconds. Self-checked by 59 suites / 4,178 executable assertions in about 300 seconds.
description.zh: 一个记忆插件顶三个：8 个统一 memory_* 工具 + 一段 1,266 字符常驻注入，主库仍是 meow-memory 的七层 SQLite，星图退成可重建的索引。工具 schema 56,759 B → 14,494 B（−74.5%），常驻注入 4,085 → 1,266 字符（−69.0%）。能力一条没砍：写入先落主库，连不上星图的连线排队不丢，设置页改完即刻生效、不用重启。0.4.0 又加了查询分解、写入巩固、自动取代与通胀体检、实体层、以及从你自己的 keywords 学出来的共现扩词——每一件都有开关，也都有开/关对照读数；0.5.0 用 CJK 词形桥让换说法也能落地。0.6.0 让打分随库规模自适应：660 条快照上照抄 hit@1 0.895 → 0.921、换说法 0.333 → 0.417、误伤 0，每条命中顺带带 `status`。0.6.1 把「三棵树没同步」做成一条命令（`tools/sync-trees.mjs`，默认只体检、从不删除），用两条静态正则钉住自适应 idf 的接线点（判据全绿但行为回退这种沉默故障过不去），并修掉一个维护脚本的 `%20` 路径 bug——引擎字节未变。0.6.2 修的是一个把「有」说成「没有」的缺陷：噪声地板剔掉了唯一能命中的词、留下库里根本不存在（df=0）的词顶位，1,531 条英文问句里 8 条回执为空；处方只救被噪声地板剔掉的词（虚词一个都不救），空回 0.52% → 0，hit@1/5/10/20、MRR 与 660 条快照三档读数逐位不变。0.6.3 让答案是可复现的：分数并列时以前会退回语料顺序（V8 稳定排序），同一个问句能因为存储布局不同给出两套前十；定序梯子现在末尾是「更新得更晚的在前」+ id 自然序，自适应 idf 挑簇不再按数组下标破平，整条链上也没有 localeCompare——所有读数逐位不变。0.6.4 修的是「一个汉字也是问题」：分词只产二元组，一个汉字的问句切出来是空数组，检索的第一道门就把「切不出词」当成「没有」，于是 `读`/`钱`/`花` 这类最直白的问法永远空手。现在只在「切不出词 + 单个汉字」时按原文子串在标题、正文与关键词里找一次，仍走同一套定序；英文停用词与标点一个都不放行。所有读数逐位不变——修的是可达性，不是排序。0.6.5 修的是「标点也是人打的」：0.6.4 的单字兜底只认「正好一个码点」，可人问一个字的时候问号几乎从不缺席——`读？`、`钱。`、`花！`、`「读」` 一个都回不来。现在把标点与空白剥掉再数，剥完正好剩一个汉字才走兜底，汉字之外只许标点或空白；字母、数字、符号一律不放行，同一个字重复按一个算。所有读数又是一位没动——修的仍是可达性，不是排序。0.6.6 修的是「脏记忆不许把整次检索打成异常」：`docText` 里的 `...d.keywords` 遇上缺字段 / `null` / 逗号串（导入行、别的插件写的行、调用方自拼的 docs）会抛 `TypeError: d.keywords is not iterable`——不是少一条命中，是整次检索一个回执都拿不回来。现在 keywords 统一走 `kwList`：数组、逗号顿号串、JSON 串都认，`docText`、打分面的 `kwToks`/`kwSets`、`keywordHitScore` 与索引签名全走它（逗号串的关键词从此真进 tf-idf）。读数一位没动，修的是可达性。0.6.7 修的是「一条坏行不许把整次检索打成异常」：`docs` 里混进一条 `null` / `undefined` / 标量（半写的行、导入截断、调用方把 id 列表当 docs），`docText` 的 `d.title` 会抛 `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'title')`；`docs` 整个不是数组时死在 `docs.length`。现在两个入口都过闸 `liveDocs(docs)`：非数组回空、逐条问「是不是对象」、脏了才过滤，干净数组原样返回同一引用（索引缓存的键是内容签名，不靠身份，缓存不会被打掉）；全是坏行时回空，不把 `null` 当一条记忆打分。读数一位没动。0.6.8 治的是判据自己的寿命：版本号、支数、断言总数、耗时预算每版都在动，写成等值就每升一版必红一次（`0.2.31→35` 四遍版本等值、`0.6.2→0.6.7` 每版手工抬 `steps.length === 35 → 36` 并连带改两处手抄的「N 支 / M 条」）。现在支数是地板 `SUITE_FLOOR`（只许加不许减，减一支立刻红、加一支不必动判据），文档里「现在」的数由探针读基线合计自动对账，历史里程碑冻结自己那版的数字，版本阶梯按版本号比。引擎一个字节没动，读数逐位相同。0.6.9 先量了尺子：0.3.0 起所有对外读数都是单次、单序量出来的（语料按库里顺序、问句按夹具顺序、跑一遍取一个数），而这一路正是拿这些单次数否决过三个候选（英文词形归一、MMR、覆盖率重排）——量尺若对顺序敏感，那些「负数」里就掺着量尺自己的噪声。现在 `tools/probe-rigor.mjs` 钉住七条：连跑 3 次三档读数逐位相同（std = 0）、语料倒序、三种打乱（seed 3/11/42）、问句倒序、独立
